Among the most challenging lesions and surgeries that neurosurgeons face 
throughout their training and early years of practice, some stand out as particularly 
formidable and daunting. Petroclival meningiomas, giant aneurysms, large

throughout their training and early years of practice, some stand out as particularly 
formidable and daunting. Petroclival meningiomas, giant aneurysms, large 
arteriovenous malformations, and high-flow interposition bypasses are examples 
that come to mind. After all, these are the quintessential cases where drama is 
assured, whether in triumph or disaster. There is nothing more reinforcing to the 
learning process than the vivid memories of the surgical battlefield during residency. 
Perhaps most zealous residents look forward to scrubbing on these surgeries. They 
certainly may be eager to participate, particularly if cerebrovascular or skull base 
surgery is in their future, but I doubt very much that even the most overconfident 
among them would have the courage (or misguided desire!) to want to be a primary 
surgeon on any such cases.

I believe vestibular schwannomas have earned the right to join this elite group of 
intimidating lesions. I concede that, unless they are giant in size, they do not inspire 
quite the same emotions of fear and trepidation in the young surgeon that a large 
aneurysm might. After all, the dreaded complication of transecting the facial nerve 
during tumor dissection, while devastating to the patient, still happens in an instant, 
with a slip of a blade or an excess of traction. Yet it happens without much drama. It 
happens in silence, often with no gradual change in intraoperative monitoring, 
without a flood of blood or cardiorespiratory instability. It does not generate a 
sustained flurry of adrenaline-charged activity by everyone in the room. It easily 
goes unnoticed by all present, even the surgeon initially. Equally disappointing but 
less consequential is the sudden loss of auditory waves, and

Unless the young surgeon performs the surgery for him/herself, over and over 
again, it is simply quite difficult for even the most skilled of surgical educators to 
convey in words or through demonstration to that young surgeon all the surgical 
subtleties required for surgical success. Indeed, the surgical pearls are not obvious; 
and there are many. Even discounting the entire complex topic of surgical indications, 
the balance of wait-and-scan versus radiosurgery versus surgical resection, the 
timing of treatment, and other popular debate-generating controversies, the steps 
involved in the surgical procedure itself are difficult to completely master quickly.

A simple deviation from proper patient positioning, ignoring the importance of 
venous return, can result in cerebellar edema even before opening the dura. Placing 
the craniotomy a touch too high to access the lateral recess of the cisterna magna

Preface
The treatment of vestibular schwannomas has undergone numerous changes and 
advancements in the past century. Innovations in surgical and now microsurgical 
techniques allow for the removal of these lesions with the preservation of nearby 
cranial nerves in the majority of cases. In addition, the development of stereotactic 
radiation can provide disease control in a minimally

e removal of these lesions with the preservation of nearby 
cranial nerves in the majority of cases. In addition, the development of stereotactic 
radiation can provide disease control in a minimally invasive fashion. Further, 
improved understanding of the natural history of these tumors and the proliferation 
of cross-sectional imaging techniques allow the safe observation of selected lesions. 
Lastly, molecular and targeted therapies hold the promise to both treat these tumors 
and restore lost functions as a result of tumor growth and/or treatment. However, 
despite the increasing use of nonsurgical management strategies, surgery nonetheless 
remains an important tool in the treatment armamentarium for physicians and 
surgeons.
Advances in and the widespread use of audiovisual technology have made a 
significant impact in teaching surgical techniques in general and more specifically 
in teaching skull base surgery. Among all the surgeries that skull base surgeons 
perform on a dail

gy have made a 
significant impact in teaching surgical techniques in general and more specifically 
in teaching skull base surgery. Among all the surgeries that skull base surgeons 
perform on a daily basis, the surgery of vestibular schwannomas or so-called 
acoustic neuromas is among the most challenging for trainees, fellows, and young 
surgeons to learn and obtain experience with. This is because the hands-on training 
for these surgeries may be limited due to concerns for cosmetic outcome factors 
including hearing and facial function. Therefore, there is a need for improved 
materials to teach these surgeries. With audiovisual observation, trainees, fellows, 
and young surgeons can observe basic and complex surgeries. This operative 
audiovisual atlas, which we believe is the first of its kind, is intended to accomplish 
this pedagogical goal by enabling its viewers and readers to observe the step-by-­
step techniques of vestibular schwannoma surgery.

Introduction
Vestibular schwannomas (VS) are benign, extra-axial, encapsulated, Schwann cell 
derived neoplasms of the vestibular part of the eighth cranial nerve. Although some 
earlier reports indicated that the superior vestibular nerve is the more common ori-
gin of VS, recent studies suggest otherwise. Sanna et al. found that the most com-
mon origin for VS are the nerve sheath of the inferior vestibular nerve, and less 
frequently the superior vestibular nerve [1]. Eighth cranial nerve schwannomas rep-
resent 90% of all intracranial nerve sheath tumors [2]. VS account for approxi-
mately 6–8% of intracranial tumors in adults [3, 4] and are the most common tumor 
in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) ranging between 80% and 95% [5, 6], followed 
by meningiomas ranging between 5% and 10% and epidermoid tumors ranging 
between 4% and 7% [7–9]. There are two types of VS; sporadic and familial. The 
sporadic form of

80% and 95% [5, 6], followed 
by meningiomas ranging between 5% and 10% and epidermoid tumors ranging 
between 4% and 7% [7–9]. There are two types of VS; sporadic and familial. The 
sporadic form of VS is commonly seen in adults and is very rare in pediatric patients. 
The familial form of VS is most commonly seen in patients with neurofibromatosis 
type 2 (NF2), and is usually bilateral.
History
Various terminologies have been used to define the VS pathology, with “Acoustic 
Neuroma” the most common. Prior terminology has caused confusion regarding 
the origin, biological behavior, and natural history of VS. This confusion is now 
resolved by using the correct name of “Vestibular Schwannoma” (VS) to define 
this pathology. “Vestibular” clearly indicates the origin of the tumor as from the 
vestibular nerve, while “schwannoma” indicates that Schwann cells are the cell 
of origin.
In 1777, anatomist Eduard Sandifort was the first to recognize the VS as an 
acoustic neuroma at autopsy.

In 1777, anatomist Eduard Sandifort was the first to recognize the VS as an 
acoustic neuroma at autopsy. It was observed as a fixed and rigid tumor adjacent to 
the cochlear nerve with extension into the internal acoustic canal (IAC) and that 
caused compression on the brainstem [10]. From that time to the early twentieth 
century, acoustic neuromas were used to the define all tumors located in the CPA.

The first attempt to remove a VS in the CPA via the transcranial route was under-
taken by Von Bergmann in 1890. The patient did not survive the surgery and histo-
pathology confirmed a VS [11]. In 1894, Charles Balance performed the first 
successful removal of the CPA tumor at two separate stages [12]. Although the 
patient survived, surgery resulted in severe complications including complete facial 
palsy. Findings during this surgery which included a tight attachment to

two separate stages [12]. Although the 
patient survived, surgery resulted in severe complications including complete facial 
palsy. Findings during this surgery which included a tight attachment to the dura of 
the petrous bone and the presence of a capsule, raised some questions about the 
origin of this tumor. At that time, it was thought that this tumor might have been a 
meningioma. Because of the lack of the definite diagnosis of this tumor, Thomas 
Annandale’s surgery in 1895 is considered as the first successful resection attempt 
to remove a VS [10, 11, 13]. In 1905, Victor Horsley performed a gross total resec-
tion of a VS that unfortunately resulted in severe postoperative brain ischemia [14]. 
Since then, many cases have been reported with high mortality and morbidity. In the 
early twentieth century, morbidity and mortality following VS surgery were still 
unfavorable, ranging between 67% and 84% [15]. Paramedian suboccipital crani-

otomy was the only approach to the VS, with manual resection of the tumor using

In 1936, Cushing introduced a new surgical technique. This consisted of a 
“T-shape” skin incision that included a horizontal incision between both mastoid 
notches, and a vertical incision from the midline to the middle level of the cervical 
spine. After this extensive skin incision, Cushing performed a large bilateral poste-
rior fossa craniectomy that exposed both CPAs laterally, the cervicomedullary junc-
tion and the cisterna magna inferiorly, and the venous sinuses superiorly. Cushing’s 
novel approach allowed a wider surgical working area, provided cerebellar relax-
ation through CSF drainage from the cisterna magna, and mobilization of the cere-
bellum and the brainstem. Thus, neuro-vascular structures became

er surgical working area, provided cerebellar relax-
ation through CSF drainage from the cisterna magna, and mobilization of the cere-
bellum and the brainstem. Thus, neuro-vascular structures became more mobile and 
were less affected by surgical maneuvers. Dandy modified Cushing’s technique, and 
hypothesized that total resection of the tumor would decrease the rates of recurrence 
and increase the long-term survival [16]. He performed more aggressive internal 
debulking to create free space and created a cleavage plane to pull the tumor capsule 
away from surrounding structures for circumferential dissection. Dandy also 
reported the first surgical series of VS in which the tumors were removed gross 
totally [16].
The next stage in the history of VS surgery was to achieve higher surgical resec-
tion rates with lower morbidity and mortality rates. In 1949, Horrax and Poppen 
reported mortality rate of 10.8% in patients with VS after gross total resection [17].

Epidemiology
Vestibular schwannomas constitute 6% of all intracranial neoplasms [4] and are the 
most common benign lesions of the IAC and CPA cistern constituting between 60% 
and 90% of the entire lesions seen in this area [20, 21]. VS are most commonly 
diagnosed in adults, and the median age of diagnosis is ranging between 52 and 
55 years in different studies [22]. These tumors are located unilaterally in more than 
90% of cases [23]. Both si

only 
diagnosed in adults, and the median age of diagnosis is ranging between 52 and 
55 years in different studies [22]. These tumors are located unilaterally in more than 
90% of cases [23]. Both sides are affected with equal frequency. Bilateral vestibular 
schwannomas are seen in patients with neurofibromatosis type 2 in the pediatric 
population as well as in the adults [24].
According to recent population-based studies, the overall incidence of VS is 
9–13 cases per million persons per year [25–27]. This translates to about 3000 cases 
per year within the United States, a number that is consistent with clinical experi-
ence. However, these population-based studies likely underestimate the incidence, 
since in the pre and early magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) era, diagnostic cross-
sectional imaging capable of detecting small lesions was unavailable or uncom-
monly performed. Contemporary MRI technology is faster and less expensive than 
previously, and is capable of detecting sm

ectional imaging capable of detecting small lesions was unavailable or uncom-
monly performed. Contemporary MRI technology is faster and less expensive than 
previously, and is capable of detecting small lesions. Recent reports have docu-
mented the capability to identify small lesion without the use of paramagnetic con-
trast material [28, 29]. Thus, it is expected that with this more sensitive diagnostic 
imaging, the incidence of VS, asymptomatic or symptomatic, will increase. Indeed, 
Anderson and colleagues found that a rate of asymptomatic VS was 0.7% per 10,000 
MRI images obtained for reasons other than assessing for CPA lesions [30]. 
Similarly, Lin and colleagues found a rate of two incidental VS findings per 10,000 
persons when they interpreted >46,000 MRI studies [31]. Likely related to the 
increasing incidence of VS over time (due to improved imaging techniques), the 
average size of the lesion at diagnosis appears to be decreasing. Stangerup and col-
leagues reported th

increasing incidence of VS over time (due to improved imaging techniques), the 
average size of the lesion at diagnosis appears to be decreasing. Stangerup and col-
leagues reported that when assessing 30 years of data from a national population 
sample size, tumor size decreased from ~3 cm in the 1970s to ~1 cm in the mid-

of increased diagnostic imaging sensitivity and the increased use of MRI for more 
indications.

infusion of 5-bromodeoxyuridine, and flow cytometric analysis. Tumor growth

Molecular Biology of Vestibular Schwannoma
The neurofibromin 2 gene is located on chromosome 22 (22q12) and produces a cell 
membrane-related protein known as merlin or schwannomin. This end-product of 
the NF2 gene is a tumor suppressor protein. Biallelic dysfunction of NF2 gene 
induces neoplastic transformation and thus results in tumor development. Both VS 
and NF2 syndrome have a close pathophysiological relationship which is linked to 
the disruption of the NF2 gene. The unilateral VS are sporadic whereas bilateral 
ones are human NF2 gene-associated schwannomas [64–66]. Bila

close pathophysiological relationship which is linked to 
the disruption of the NF2 gene. The unilateral VS are sporadic whereas bilateral 
ones are human NF2 gene-associated schwannomas [64–66]. Bilateral VS have the 
distinctive characteristic feature of NF2.
Radiology
Early diagnosis plays an important role in the outcome of VS, especially with high 
resolution detection of small tumors. MRI is the radiological test of choice for the 
evaluation of VS. Although MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis and surgical 
planning, computerized tomography (CT) is also an important diagnostic tool to 
evaluate bony anatomy. CT is also useful to demonstrate the skull base, secondary 
bony changes such as the degree of enlargement of the IAC, any erosion of the 
medial petrous bone, and the level of the jugular bulb. VS appear as isodense and 
isointense lesions on non-contrast CT and T1-weighted MRI, respectively. They 
show mostly homogenous enhancement, although heterogenous enhancement wit

of the jugular bulb. VS appear as isodense and 
isointense lesions on non-contrast CT and T1-weighted MRI, respectively. They 
show mostly homogenous enhancement, although heterogenous enhancement with 
contrast is not uncommon. They appear as hyperintense on T2-weighted images. 
Large to very large VS may be associated with surrounding vasogenic edema in the 
cerebellum and brain stem. Tumors larger than 2.5 cm in size are commonly associ-
ated with brain stem compression and hydrocephalus.

Treatment Alternatives and Surgical Decision
Treatment alternatives for VS include observation, surgical removal, radiation and a 
combination of surgery and radiation. We believe treatment should be tailored to the 
patient on an individual basis, and that algorithms should be avoided. This is because 
the range of variables for each patient with VS is too large for algorithms to have 
significant utility.
Observation
Older asymptomatic patients and patients with intracanalicular VS are, in general, 
candidates for observation. In a Sanna et al. report that examined 576 VS patients 
with a 27 year follow-up, 84 of 154 (54.5%) tumors with 5-year follow-up showed 
no growth, 12 of them (8%) showed slow growth, and 2 (1.3%) of the patients 
showed fast growth rates [67]. The psychological make-up of each individual patient 
also plays an important role in treatment decision-making and during fol

showed fast growth rates [67]. The psychological make-up of each individual patient 
also plays an important role in treatment decision-making and during follow-up. 
With young patients that have small to moderate size tumors, radiological imaging 
and audiometry should be performed in close intervals. Again, the follow-up plan 
should be individualized for each patient.
Surgery
Surgery remains the main treatment of choice for many patients, regardless of the size 
of the tumor, since surgery can provide a cure with a reasonably low risk. Gross total 
resection is the goal of surgery while maintaining good facial function in all sizes of 
tumors, and hearing preservation in small to moderate size tumors in patients with 
serviceable preoperative hearing status. There are three main types of surgical 
approaches in the microsurgical treatment of VS, which include the retrosigmoid, the 
translabyrinthine, and the middle cranial fossa approaches

Radiation
Radiation is an effective treatment for small to moderate size VS with good long-­
term tumor control. However, there are few studies of follow-up that are longer than

Introduction
The neurology pertinent to the diagnosis, evaluation and treatment of vestibular 
schwannomas (VSs) is reviewed in this chapter. This begins with a discussion of the 
normal anatomy and physiology of inner ear, anatomy of the vestibulocochlear 
nerve (VCN), anatomy and physiology of the facial nerve (FN), includes a discus-
sion of the clinical manifestations of the lesions, history and physical examinations, 
diagnostic testing commonly employed in contemporary practice. The chapter con-
cludes with a discussion about intraoperative monitoring techniques typically

Anatomy
The clinical manifestations of VSs depend on both the size of the lesion and its loca-
tion relative to surrounding neurovascular structures. Schwannomas can arise from 
other nerves in the region and present with similar symptoms but these are uncom-
mon and beyond the scope of this textbook. VSs are benign tumors that arise from 
the superior or inferior vestibular nerves. These nerves originate from the lateral 
aspect of the brainstem, traverse the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) cistern and the 
internal acoustic canal (IAC) of the temporal bone and terminate in the inner ear,

the central nervous system structures and bony confines of the cranial vault. There 
are two cisterns that are of primary importance to vestibular schwannoma treatment: 
the CPA and prepontine (PP) cisterns. The CPA cistern is an expansion of the sub-
arachnoid space between the lateral lobe of the cerebellum, cerebellar peduncles,

most patients, the posterior petrous apex is typically quite small. Laterally, the 
IAC terminates at the fundus and the FN and VCNs enter the otic capsule. The otic

Facial Nerve Anatomy and Physiology
The FN courses from its brainstem nuclei in the inferior pons and medulla oblon-
gata, through the CPA cistern, the IAC, the otic capsule, the middle ear and mastoid 
and finally into the face and upper neck. It provides afferent and efferent innervation 
to a variety of structures and locations in the skull, face, and neck. Given its proxim-
ity to the VCN in the CPA cistern and IAC, the facial nerve is at risk for damage 
during surgical treatment of VSs. The pertinent anatomy and neurology will be 
reviewed in the sections below.

Finally, there are three layers of fascia/connective tissue that invest the facial 
nerve: endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium. The endoneurium is tightly 
adherent to the myelin that surrounds each myelinated nerve fiber. The perineurium 
is connective tissue that surrounds distinct groups of fibers (called fascials). The 
epineurium surrounds and separates the fascials and surrounds the entire nerve. The 
cisternal portion of the FN does not have an epineurial layer and this has important 
implications. The lack of a protective epineurium makes the nerve more prone to 
surgical injury during surgery. Additionally, the lack of epineurium allows the indi-
vidual nerve fascials to occasionally splay over the surface of an expanding lesion, 
making identification and separation of the FN and the tumor much more difficult.

Hearing Physiology
Sound energy is transferred to the inner ear via the auricle (aka, pinna), external 
auditory canal (EAC), tympanic membrane (TM), and ossicles (malleus, incus and 
stapes). This energy reaches cochlea, where specialized mechanoreceptors (hair 
cells) on the basilar membrane stimulate bipolar spiral ganglion neurons. Hair cells 
derive their name from the several rows cilia that extend up from the apical surface. 
The basilar membrane varies in thickness, width and stiffness in a progressive fash-
ion from base to apex that creates a tonotopic representation of sound frequency, 
call tonotopy. High frequency sounds are detecte

ion from base to apex that creates a tonotopic representation of sound frequency, 
call tonotopy. High frequency sounds are detected at the base and low frequency 
sounds are detected at the apex with a gradient between each end. This tonotopic 
arrangement allows the cochlea to serve as a frequency analyzer for incident sound 
energies. When the basilar membrane moves in response to sound, this results in 
movement of the cilia of each hair cell and this movement converts the mechanical 
movement into voltage changes and ultimately, neurotransmitter release. Each hair 
cell on the basilar membrane is innervated by several spiral ganglion cells. These 
nerve fibers combine together to form the cochlear portion of VCN, which joins 
with the VNs to form the main trunk of VCN as it traverses the IAC and CPA cis-
tern. The spiral ganglion cells primarily project to cells in the cochlear nucleus,

cule. The utricle detects horizontal linear acceleration (anterior, posterior, and lat-
eral translational movements) and the saccule detects vertical linear acceleration

the stapedial muscle, which when contracting, tenses and increases the impedance 
of the ossicular chain. This reflex is bilateral, meaning that when activated in one

Intraoperative Monitoring
Depending on the goals of surgery and the surgical approach selected by the patient 
and surgeon, various cranial nerves may be monitored during the operation. The 
most common nerves that are monitored include cranial nerve VII and VIII but the 
lower cranial nerves can be monitored as well.
Cranial Nerve VII

of vestibular schwannoma and is particularly useful in medium and large sized 
tumors. Its main uses include monitoring for possible facial nerve (FN) injury and 
physiologic identification in situations where the FN anatomy has been significantly 
altered. However, FNM does not replace the detailed anatomic knowledge and tech-
nical skill required to operate near the facial nerve.

Auditory brainstem response and cochlear nerve action potential testing measure 
auditory evoked potentials (AEPs), electrical potentials generated by populations of 
neurons responding to acoustic stimuli. AEPs provide measures of the electrophysi-

the health of the auditory neuroanatomy. During microsurgical treatment of VS,

Auditory evoked potentials are generated by synchronized firing of large popula-

cochlea and the neurons of the central auditory system [48, 62–65]. Specifically, an 
acoustic stimulus is presented to the outer ear and the electrical responses (voltage 
changes) resulting from the acoustically responsive elements (hair cells and neuron) 
are measured over time. Each stage of acoustic processing generates a characteristic 
response characterized by specific morphology (shape, polarity and amplitude of 
the response) and timing in relationship to the stimulus (latency) [65]. AEPs are 
very small, normally in the microvolt or nanovolt range [48, 52] and as such, spe-
cialized technical and processing strategies are employed to detect these signals.

are located at a distance from the neural generators of the AEP signals [48, 49, 65]. 
Advantages of BAER include the familiarity of BAER waveforms to most surgeons 
and neurophysiologists, the capacity to obtain preoperative measurements, consis-

recording environment as the electrodes are located away from the operative field.

the measured responses (nanovolts to microvolts). This results in a need for signifi-

take a considerable amount of time and reduces the temporal accuracy of BAER

The ultimate goal of undertaking a hearing preserving surgical approach is to 
preserve hearing, not intraoperative AEP responses. The presence of AEP responses 
is not perfectly predictive of postoperative hearing [50, 54, 57, 60] and the loss of 
AEP responses does not preclude postoperative hearing [54–59]. The overall trend 
in the literature over the past 40 years has been that intraoperative AEP monitoring 
is reported to be useful [26, 52–54, 57, 59, 60, 68, 72, 73, 76, 80, 82, 83, 87–90], 
though this is a source of controversy and not uniformly supported [60, 66, 91, 92]. 
When consider BAER, the most consistent and established prognostic finding is that 
the presence of a stable wave V is associated with preserved hearing of some con-
figuration [50, 51, 53, 59, 68, 74, 88, 90, 93]. The prognostic value of CNAP 
respons

hed prognostic finding is that 
the presence of a stable wave V is associated with preserved hearing of some con-
figuration [50, 51, 53, 59, 68, 74, 88, 90, 93]. The prognostic value of CNAP 
responses have also been generally reported to useful and predictive of postopera-
tive hearing. Most authors report a favorable prognosis for postoperative hearing if 
CNAP is present at the end of the case [26, 54, 59, 73, 83, 87]. When comparing 
BAER to CNAP, the majority of the published reports either find that CNAP is bet-
ter than BAER or that the addition of CNAP to BAER is beneficial to the postopera-
tive hearing outcome [26, 54, 59, 73, 75, 76, 80, 82, 83, 87].

Introduction
Since the technical description by William House [1] in 1961, the middle cranial 
fossa (MCF) approach to the internal acoustic canal (IAC) has become one of the 
quintessential surgical approaches for accessing the 7th and 8th cranial nerves and 
the upper cerebellopontine angle (CPA). Though many variations have been 
described, in this chapter the MCF approach comprises an extradural, subtemporal 
exposure and removal of a portion of the superior surface of the temporal bone to 
expose the posterior cranial fossa (PCF) structures. The technique affords access to 
the entire contents of the internal acoustic canal (IAC) and can allow for hearing 
preservation by avoiding violation of the otic capsule during the surgical exposure.

The patient with a small vestibular schwannoma (VS) that does not impact the brain-
stem and who demonstrates good hearing, presents a formidable management chal-
lenge to the contemporary skull base surgeon due to the variety of treatment options 
available and evolving patient preferences and expectations. This is especially true 
for patients who are candidates for a hearing preserving treatment as these patients 
often have few, if any symptoms. In properly selected patients, surgical excision via 
a middle cranial fossa approach to the IAC can provide excellent tumor control while 
maximizing the preservation of residual cranial nerve function.

A Brief History of the Middle Cranial Fossa Approach 
to the Skull Base
The MCF approach to the IAC and CPA has a long and storied history and includes 
some of the most famous surgeons in both neurotology and neurosurgery. Early 
descriptions of exposing PCF contents through the extradural, subtemporal MCF 
route focused on treating trigeminal neuralgia by targeting the Gasserian ganglion 
and its major divisions or deeply seated temporal bone infections [2]. Early reports 
by Horsley (1891) and Hartley (1892) describe intradural and extradural exposures, 
respectively, of the Gasserian ganglion but initial results were highly morbid or mor-
tal [3, 4]. Krause described an extradural approach to the Gasserian ganglion similar 
in technique and around the same time as Hartley [5]. This extradural approach 
became known as the Hartley-Krause procedure and with modifications by Cushing 
(1900), such as preservation of the middle meningeal artery, it became the mainstay 
of t

(1900), such as preservation of the middle meningeal artery, it became the mainstay 
of trigeminal neuralgia surgery during the first half of the twentieth century [2, 5–7]. 
Around the same time as the MCF approach was being used to treat trigeminal neu-
ralgia, von Bergmann devised and Körner popularized an extradural subtemporal 
approach to treat otogenic intracranial infections by elevating the dura from the 
upper surface of the temporal bone and then chiseling down from the tegmen to 
address the intratemporal infection [2].
The first description of the MCF approach to the IAC was described by Parry 
(1904) for the treatment of intractable tinnitus and episodic vertigo by sectioning of 
the vestibulocochlear nerve [8]. Parry described the creation of an inferiorly based 
osteocutaneous flap for exposure of the MCF, careful elevation of the dura from the

superior surface of the temporal bone, opening of the middle ear and mastoid to 
ensure no active infection, and then removal of the roof of the IAC to expose the 
cranial nerves within the IAC for sectioning. It is notable that while the operation 
was a technical success (CN VIII was sectioned easily), the procedure was compli-
cated with the inadvertent transection of the facial nerve.
As reviewed by Moonfaced et  al. (2010), the extradural subtemporal MCF 
approach was utilized for the intracranial treatment of variety of disorders related to 
hearing and balance [2]. Holmgren (1917) in Sweden proposed treating otosclerosis 
with superior semicircular canal fenestration through a MCF exposure [2]. Putnam 
(1938), a former student of Cushing, attempted to treat intractable vertigo with laby-

that the structures are encountered or traversed.

•	 We generally limit the middle cranial fossa approach to those under 65 years of

floor in older individuals;

Contraindications
There are no absolute contraindications to the middle fossa approach to the IAC. 
Relative contraindications include:
•	 Inability to tolerate a major surgical (intracranial) procedure;
•	 Age 65 years or greater;
•	 Non-socially useful hearing (AAO-HNS CHE Class C-D or WRS III-IV);

The preoperative evaluation consists of diagnostic testing to establish the identity 
and location of the lesion, pure-tone and speech audiometry to determine residual 
hearing ability and classification, auditory evoked electrical potential testing if 
intraoperative evoked potential monitoring is to be utilized, and the testing to ensure 
that the patient is an appropriate surgical candidate. Imaging of the skull base anat-

Auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) can be utilized for intraoperative monitoring 
of the residual hearing. The basis of how AEPs are generated and used are reviewed 
in Chap. 2. The most commonly employed AEPs utilized during MCF microsurgical 
treatment of VSs are the brainstem auditory evoked response (BAER) and the 
cochlear nerve action potential (CNAP). BAERs are electrical waves of synchronized 
electrical activity generated from different peripheral and central auditory system 
locations in response to an acoustic stimulus. Preoperative BAER testing can be 
helpful as if no discernable waveforms are present, then this can indicate that 
intraoperative monitoring may be limited value. The CNAP cannot be measured 
preoperatively as reviewed in Chap. 2.

Results
The main outcomes for surgical removal of vestibular schwannoma include 
tumor removal and recurrence, facial nerve function, and the occurrence of 
complications such as CSF leakage, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, dys-
phasia, seizure, headache, deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolus and death.

As discussed previously, retention of postoperative hearing is important but is 
considered a lower surgical priority than tumor removal and facial nerve func-
tion. Major complications such as meningitis, intracranial hemorrhage, seizures, 
aphasias are rare in contemporary practice [14, 15, 53, 69–72]. Cerebrospinal 
fluid leakage rates from larger patient series range from 5% to 9% and are typi-
cally managed with CSF diversion though, wound exploration is occasionally 
needed [15, 70, 71].
Facial nerve outcomes are generally quite favorable and are typically equivalent 
to those obtained with the translabyrinthine exposure. Most contemporary studies 
report that long-term HB score of I or II of ~90% of greater [15, 69–72]. In one large 
study looking exclusively at surgical management via the MCF approach, Meyer 
and colleagues reported on 162 consecutive patients who underwent surgery and

Abstract
The retrosigmoid approach offers hearing preservation for small and medium-­
sized vestibular schwannomas while providing excellent exposure of the cerebel-
lopontine angle and lateral cerebellomedullary cisterns that contain critical 
neurovascular structures. A 3 × 3 cm retrosigmoid craniotomy with exposure of 
the TSSJ and an approximately 1/4 of the medial border of the sigmoid sinus is

A 3 × 3 cm retrosigmoid craniotomy with exposure of 
the TSSJ and an approximately 1/4 of the medial border of the sigmoid sinus is 
sufficient enough in many cases of VS surgeries. With small and medium-sized 
tumors, the initial exposure of the tumor includes its lateral part of the tumor, the 
AICA and its subarcuate branch, the lower cranial nerves and the PICA in the 
inferior aspect of the tumor, as well as the petrosal vein in the rostral aspect. 
Good postoperative FN function can be achieved by, maintaining the blood sup-
ply of the FN, minimizing bipolar coagulation around the nerve, preserving the 
arachnoid plane between the tumor and the FN, and keeping the tumor capsule 
intact during internal decompression. Surgical precautions to achieve a better 
postoperative hearing outcome include; gentle manipulation of the CoN, obtain-

Introduction
There are several important factors influencing the selection of the surgical approach 
for vestibular schwannomas (VS). These include the size of the tumor in the internal 
acoustic canal (IAC), the extent of the tumor’s impingement on the brainstem, the 
patient’s hearing and general health, and the preference and experience of the surgi-
cal team. The goal of surgical treatment should be a total tumor resection while 
preserving neurological functions. The retrosigmoid approach (RA) offers hearing 
preservation for small and medium-sized VSs while providing excellent exposure of 
the cerebellopontine angle and lateral cerebello-m

ological functions. The retrosigmoid approach (RA) offers hearing 
preservation for small and medium-sized VSs while providing excellent exposure of 
the cerebellopontine angle and lateral cerebello-medullary cisterns that contain 
important neurovascular structures including the lower cranial nerves, the posterior 
inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), and 
the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves (FN and VCN, respectively). However, the 
chance of leaving a residual tumor might be higher with a RA since visualization of 
the lateral aspect of the IAC is limited even with drilling of the IAC. Although the 
RA is well-suited to tumors of any size, regardless of the preoperative hearing sta-
tus, tumors that spare the lateral one third of the IAC and that do not impinge upon 
the brainstem, provide the best cases for hearing preservation.

Surgical Technique
Long-term muscle relaxants should be avoided during the induction of anesthesia 
since these may interfere with monitoring of the FN. Following the induction of 
anesthesia and endotracheal intubation, a urinary catheter and an arterial line are 
placed. The patient is then hyperventilated to achieve an arterial PaCO2 between 28 
and 32 mmHg. Intravenous infusion of prophylactic antibiotics are begun half an 
hour prior to skin incision, with repetitive doses administered as necessary depend-
ing on the length of the surgery. Dexamethasone (10 mg) and mannitol (0.5–1 g/kg 
of 20% solution) are given intravenously for brain relaxation. All pressure points are 
padded and sequential compression devices are placed around the patient’s legs and 
switched on. Although the placement of a lumbar drain is optional, we routinely 
place a lumbar drain in patients with all sizes of VS

ial compression devices are placed around the patient’s legs and 
switched on. Although the placement of a lumbar drain is optional, we routinely 
place a lumbar drain in patients with all sizes of VSs in order to prevent postopera-
tive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage.

tumors of any size. For this purpose, continuous intraoperative monitoring of the FN 
are obtained from the orbicularis oculi and orbicularis oris muscles via needle elec-

The brainstem auditory evoked responses (BAER) are monitored via electrodes 
inserted in the external auditory canal and on the cranial vertex in patients for whom 
hearing preservation is attempted.

patients without preoperative tinnitus suffer from it in the postoperative period, 
while more than 50% of patients complaining of tinnitus experience a significant 
improvement after surgery [113]. Although daily activities are not seriously affected 
[96], patients’ quality of life is lowered in the presence of tinnitus [114, 115, 117].

the limited exposure of the IAC and blind dissection of the IAC fundus during sur-

Serial gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the modality of choice in both detection

common finding within the first year of surgery, usually reflects the inflammation 
and scar formation due to surgery, while nodular enhancement should raise suspi-

Patient Selection
The most common indication for translabyrinthine (TL) surgery is a vestibular 
schwannoma (VS) of any size in an ear with nonserviceable hearing [1, 2]. 
Controversy persists in approach selection for patients with good hearing and larger 
tumors (greater than 2 cm of cerebellopontine angle (CPA) tumor component) [3]. 
Some institutions may favor a TL approach for these tumors because the rate of 
hearing preservation

Some institutions may favor a TL approach for these tumors because the rate of

approach even in patients with larger tumors (up to 3 cm in diameter) who have an 
SRT < 30 db and word recognition >70%. Several variables, including patient char-

must be taken into consideration when deciding on a TL approach.
Small tumors located in the internal acoustic canal (IAC) with less than 5 mm of 
extension in the CPA are best treated with a middle cranial fossa (MCF) approach if 
there is serviceable hearing [4]. Small to medium tumors measuring up to 2 cm in diam-

there is serviceable hearing [4]. Small to medium tumors measuring up to 2 cm in diam-
eter with good hearing are ideally suited to a retrosigmoid approach (RA) with hearing 
preservation and endoscopic assistance depending on tumor characteristics [5]. The 
presence of good cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at the fundus of the IAC is a favorable prog-
nostic factor. The TL approach is often preferred with tumors larger than 2 cm since the 
hearing preservation rate is low and the procedure may be better tolerated than a RA 
particularly in older, more frail patients even if there is serviceable hearing [6].
Advantages and Disadvantages of the Translabyrinthine 
Approach
There are several advantages to the TL approach when compared with other routes 
to the posterior cranial base. In comparison to the RA, it offers direct complete 
exposure of the IAC. The TL approach also offers better anterior and superior

The TL approach offers good flexibility and may be extended and combined with

Finally, the approach may be combined with a retrosigmoid technique by ligating

The primary disadvantage of this approach is the obvious loss of hearing. In 
larger tumors, with a wide inferior brain stem attachment, a high jugular bulb can 
limit the surgical exposure [8]. This route is contraindicated in patients with active 
chronic otitis media and mastoiditis.
Preoperative Preparation
A thorough otologic and neurotologic history and physical examination should 
be performed on all patients. The patient’s subjective assessment of hearing, dis-
equilibrium, imbalance, and tinnitus intensity are reviewed. A comprehensive 
neurological review of systems should be included, with particular attention to 
any cranial nerve

sment of hearing, dis-
equilibrium, imbalance, and tinnitus intensity are reviewed. A comprehensive 
neurological review of systems should be included, with particular attention to 
any cranial nerve symptoms. A past medical history of chronic ear disease or 
prior otologic surgery should be elicited. A family history of intracranial neo-
plasm or neurofibromatosis is of obvious importance. In addition to the standard 
otologic and head and neck examination, cranial nerve function and vestibular 
function should be assessed. Subtle physical findings may include a diminished 
corneal reflex, reduced sensation of the ear canal or drift and past-pointing to the 
ipsilateral side.
All patients undergo complete audiometric testing, including pure tone and speech 
audiometry. Electrocochleography (ECoG) and auditory brain stem response (ABR) 
testing are performed as a preoperative baseline if hearing preservation is being con-
sidered. Preoperative vestibular testing, including videonystagm

y (ECoG) and auditory brain stem response (ABR) 
testing are performed as a preoperative baseline if hearing preservation is being con-
sidered. Preoperative vestibular testing, including videonystagmography (VNG), is 
also useful. Preoperative evaluation by the balance physical therapy team, including 
platform posturography, may prove useful in selected patients who require vestibular 
retraining postoperatively. All patients undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) 
with contrast enhancement. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the 
temporal bone is not required but may delineate anatomical abnormalities, including 
a high jugular bulb, sclerotic mastoid, or anteriorly placed sigmoid sinus. Widening 
of the IAC also correlates negatively with hearing preservation. MRI with neuronavi-
gation protocol may be useful if intraoperative navigation is planned in more com-
plex tumors.

Operative Procedure
The TL procedure should be performed in a large operating suite that provides 
ample room for equipment, including the operating microscope, intraoperative 
monitoring systems, neuronavigation, dissection tools, high-speed drills, and cavi-
tating ultrasonic aspirators. Increased room size is also needed for added personnel, 
including neuroanesthesia and nursing staff, the multidisciplinary surgical team, 
intraoperative monitoring personnel, and observers.
For the routine TL approach, the head is rotated around 60–80° to the contralat-
eral side, with the chin gently flexed toward the shoulder [8]. The surgeon is seated 
on the same side as the anesthesiologist, who is located toward the feet. The operat-
ing room nurse is positioned directly across from the surgeon. The first assistant and 
microscope

geon is seated 
on the same side as the anesthesiologist, who is located toward the feet. The operat-
ing room nurse is positioned directly across from the surgeon. The first assistant and 
microscope base are positioned at the head of the table. Arterial line placement and 
facial nerve monitoring are always performed. Intravenous mannitol (0.5–1.0 g/kg) 
and dexamethasone are given for larger tumors.
A limited hair clipping is performed and adhesive drapes are applied. A pre-
vious abdominal incision or the left lower quadrant is also prepared for harvest-

is infiltrated with 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine prior to the skin 
prep. Although lumbar drainage

Postoperative Management
In our experience, the TL approach to the IAC has the lowest rate of CSF leakage. 
This is most likely due to the fact that we now close the eustachian tube through the 
facial recess approach in all cases. If it occurs, initial treatment of CSF leakage 
consists of bed rest and lumbar drainage. However, for the last 3 years, we routinely 
place lumbar drain in all VS cases.
The overall incidence of facial paresis has been dramatically reduced over the 
past 25  years. New techniques in tumor debulking, sharp dissection, and 
intraoperative facial nerve monitoring have led to excellent rates of facial nerve 
preservation [9]. Despite these results, iatrogenic injury to the facial nerve does 
occur. Complete facial nerve decompression of the labyrinthine segment and

perigeniculate region is facilitated with the TL approach. Transtemporal rerouting

Intraoperative facial nerve monitoring may be useful as a predictor of postoperative

Abstract
Surgical approaches for the treatment of complex vestibular schwannoma (VS) 
cases are discussed with a case-based discussion. Subtotal resection or staged 
resection should be considered to minimize the risk of cranial nerve and/or other 
neural injury in complex cases. Complicating factors include anatomical varia-
tions such as a high-riding jugular bulb, a forward-riding sigmoid sinus which 
narrows the presigmoid exposure, small and/or contracted mastoid bone, a previ-
ously thrombosed or absent sigmoid sinus on the contralateral side. Additional 
factors may include cystic schwannomas, tumors with brainstem compression 
and associated hydrocephalus, comorbid diseases that complicate anesthesia, 
prior history of VS surgery or radiation therapy, and rapid tumor progression 
associated with intratumoral hemorrhage. We have discussed and

prior history of VS surgery or radiation therapy, and rapid tumor progression 
associated with intratumoral hemorrhage. We have discussed and provided 
examples of the surgical approaches and considerations for the treatment of com-
plex vestibular schwannomas through five case illustrations. The surgical team 
should consider, especially when difficulties arise, if the surgery should be staged

achieving total resection to reduce the potential of damage to the critical

Introduction
In this chapter, we will address surgical approaches for the treatment of complex 
vestibular schwannoma cases (VS) with a case-based discussion. The complexity of 
the surgical technique for VSs stem from multiple factors, including tumor size, ana-
tomical variations, hearing status of the patient, tumor’s relation with critical neuro-
vascular structures, the patient’s wishes, and prior surgical or radiation history [1, 2].
The size of the VS is the most important factor determining the complexity of th

The size of the VS is the most important factor determining the complexity of the 
surgery and the influence on the outcome. Large VSs differ from small and medium 
VSs in terms of accompanying pathoanatomical changes. The high long-term pressure 
from a large VS to neurovascular structures in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) is a 
critical factor for the entire pathologic cascade. Such mechanical effects increase the 
susceptibility of neural structures to injury, disrupts the natural anatomical spaces, and 
limits potential surgical dissection planes. As a result, important neural structures 
become more susceptible to mechanical effects and are more prone to injury during 
surgery. Therefore, in some of these cases, subtotal resection or staged resection should 
be considered to minimize the risk of cranial nerve and/or other neural injury [1, 2].

This case is presented to demonstrate difficulties inherent with large multi-cystic 
VSs. Cystic vestibular schwannomas are notorious for being adherent to both neural 
and vascular structures, poor outcomes, and sudden growth and expansion. These 
features make cystic VS cases quite challenging. When dealing with such cases, 
these points should be taken into consideration: (1) When manipulating the cystic 
part of the tumor it is important not to break the cyst wall, which may be quite thin 
in some portions, since this may result in losing the surgeons ability to handle of the 
cyst wall. (2) There are often small brainstem arteries adherent to the cyst wall. 
Dissecting these arteries free from the tumor while preserving them can be chal-
lenging. It is necessary to spend the time and make the effort to carefully dissect

rteries adherent to the cyst wall. 
Dissecting these arteries free from the tumor while preserving them can be chal-
lenging. It is necessary to spend the time and make the effort to carefully dissect and 
preserve this vasculature and remove it from the tumor capsule, assuming gross 
total resection is the desired goal of the surgery. (3) Most large VSs have some red-
colored congested veins, which are tributaries from the tumor-feeding veins between 
the tumor and the brainstem. Prematurely interrupting these veins can cause signifi-
cant bleeding. Should there be bleeding from these veins, it is best to control bleed-
ing using oxidized regenerated cellulose or other hemostatic agents since these 
veins have very fragile walls that can make it impossible to use bipolar coagulation. 
(4) It is necessary to move back and forth between different dissection planes in 
order to go all around the tumor, and to maintain continuity of the cyst walls.

This case is presented to demonstrate that some large VSs, especially in young

with hemostasis. Hypervascularity of the tumor and its capsule in the porus and 
internal acoustic canal locations are due to rich meningeal feeders coming from the

extreme care should be exercised not to use high-level bipolar coagulation near the 
facial nerve, and that only side feeders should be taken.
Summary
To sum up, we have discussed and demonstrated examples of the surgical approaches 
and considerations for the treatment of complex VSs through five case illustrations. 
The surgical team needs to contem

sum up, we have discussed and demonstrated examples of the surgical approaches 
and considerations for the treatment of complex VSs through five case illustrations. 
The surgical team needs to contemplate multiple factors in deciding upon the surgi-
cal plan, including tumor size, anatomical variations, tumor’s relation to critical 
neurovascular structures, the patient’s wishes, and prior treatment history. 
Furthermore, the team should also consider, especially when difficulties arise, if the 
surgery should be staged to improve surgical exposure, and/or if the surgery should 
be terminated without achieving total resection to reduce the potential of harm to 
the patient.

Abstract
Purpose  Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy is a common form of focal drug resistant epilepsy in adults. Various mesial temporal 
lobe structures are integral in the genesis of temporal seizures and the hippocampal sclerosis is the primary neuropathologi­
cal finding in these cases. Surgical treatment is considered the preferred management. This study aims to analyze the ana­
tomical and surgical aspects of various resection techniques of selective amygdalohippocampectomy (SAHE)and clarify the 
critical anatomical landmarks and technical nuances associated which each method.
Me

critical anatomical landmarks and technical nuances associated which each method.
Methods  Through dissection of five human head and brain specimens we evaluated three primary surgical approaches for 
SAHE—transsylvian, transcortical, and subtemporal — and additionally discussed laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT). 
We examined the anatomical considerations of the temporal lobe and its white matter tracts, as well as the technical aspects 
of each approach.
Results  The transcortical approach provides direct access to mesial structures but requires precise placement of the corticot­
omy based on hemisphere dominance to avoid arcuate fascicle and optic radiation. The subtemporal approach preserves all 
above white matter tracts but may risk interruption of the inferior longitudinal fasciculus. The transsylvian approach allows 
for comprehensive exposure but poses ris

temporal approach preserves all 
above white matter tracts but may risk interruption of the inferior longitudinal fasciculus. The transsylvian approach allows 
for comprehensive exposure but poses risks to tracts within limen insulae, namely uncinate and inferior fronto – occipital 
fascicles. Additionally, there is a risk to middle cerebral artery and its branches. LITT offers a minimally invasive alternative 
with comparable outcomes and reduced risk of cognitive side effects.
Conclusion  Selective amygdalohippocampectomy and its variants, including LITT, are surgical strategies for managing 
mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. Each approach has distinct anatomical and technical considerations that influence the choice 
of a technique. Due to complex anatomy of temporal lobe and white matter tracts variability more research is essential for 
achieving favourable outcomes.

Materials and methods
Five fresh human head and brain specimens (10 sides) were 
dissected at the Surgical Neuroanatomy Laboratory of the 
Department of Neurological Surgery at the Medical Uni­
versity of Warsaw. The common carotid arteries, vertebral 
arteries, and internal jugular veins were isolated, cannu­
lated, and injected with red and blue silicone for enhanced 
visualization. To facilitate white matter dissection, the adult 
cerebral hemispheres were prepared using Klingler’s prepa­
ration technique [8]. The cortical s

visualization. To facilitate white matter dissection, the adult 
cerebral hemispheres were prepared using Klingler’s prepa­
ration technique [8]. The cortical surface was assessed using 
the naked eye. Next, white matter dissection was performed 
using microscopic magnification and microsurgical tools to 
expose the white matter tracts and ventricular system within 
the temporal lobe. A digital camera (NikonD7200 with a 
Nikon DX 35 mm lens; 1:1.8 G) was used for image docu­
mentation. The study was approved by the Bioethics Com­

AKBE/190/2023.

Approaching the mesial temporal structures from below 
requires caution due to the proximity of white matter tracts 
such as the ILF and cingulum fibers. The ILF, which pre­
dominantly carries fibers between the occipital and tem­
poral lobes, plays an integral role in visual processing and 
object recognition [11]. Disruption of the ILF during surgi­
cal resection may lead to impairments in visual perception, 
memory, and processing of visual stimuli, especially with 
the subtemporal approach. From a technical standpoint, 
the LITT technique offers a minimally invasive approach 
that allows for the sparing of these important tracts, as it 
precisely targets the amygdala and hippocampus while

The Pathway to Competence: Understanding its origins and purpose 
Every discipline that transitions to Competence by Design (CBD) develops a Pathway to 
Competence document (the pathway) as part of the discipline’s CBD educational standards 
suite.  The pathway helps to highlight the foundational connection between CanMEDS and 
the rest of the CBD design, including stages of training, milestones and EPAs. 
The pathway illustrates the progression of a resident’s competence through 4 stages of 
training in a given discipline or special program. These stages include Transition to 
Discipline, Foundations of Discipline, Core of Discipline, and Transition to Practice. The 
pathway presents the CanMEDS milestones (observable markers) that the resident must 
acquire in order to attain the exit competencies outlined in the Discipline Competencies.

Understanding the structure and format of the Pathway to Competence document 
The Pathway to Competence is presented as a chart with the competencies, organized by 
CanMEDS Role, appearing down the y-axis, and the stages of training as columns along the 
x-axis. Each row displays the milestones for the associated enabling competency, allowing
readers to see a progression across stages. Ultimately, the Pathway to Competence also
allows for customized isolated views. For example, a preceptor can see all of the Medical
Expert milestones that a resident must achieve in the Core of Discipline stage, or she can
view the ideal progression for just one particular key competency (e.g. handover).

impact of a mass in the cerebellum belies its relatively low 
incidence, and involvement of contiguous brainstem struc­
tures significantly increases the morbidity and mortality of 
these tumors. A wide spectrum of pathologies is observed 
among cerebellar tumors. This chapter will focus on intrin­
sic cerebellar tumors in adults, with considerations for com­
monly observed extrinsic tumors, such as meningiomas or 
schwannomas, to be discussed elsewhere.
Clinical Presentation
Cerebellar tumors commonly present as one of several dis­
tinct scenarios. Headache, nausea, imbalance, and gait dys­
function are the most frequent complaints, attributable to 
mass effect and/or hydrocephalus. Involvement of the adja­
cent brainstem, tectum, and cranial nerves are less common 
presenting findings.

The cerebellum demonstrates functional localization;

important for limb ataxia. Injury to the dentate nuclei can 
lead to dysarthria and mutism in some patients.

Imaging
Upon presentation with symptoms and signs suggestive of a 
cerebellar mass, a computed tomography (CT) and/or mag­
netic resonance imaging (MRI) is typically obtained next. 
CT scans have the advantage that they can be done rapidly 
and thus help to determine immediate treatment upon initial 
presentation of the patient. MRI offers more definitive visu­
alization of the mass in determining differential diagnosis 
and surgical strategy.
Cerebellar tumors can be solid or cystic. Solid masses are 
frequently isointense to gray matter on T1-­ and T2-­weighted 
images; however, tumors such as pilocytic astrocytomas can 
appear isointense to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on T2.3,4 Highly 
cellular tumors, such as medulloblastoma, frequently demon­
strate restricted diffusion with high

cellular tumors, such as medulloblastoma, frequently demon­
strate restricted diffusion with high signal on diffusion-­weighted 
imaging and low apparent diffusion coefficient signal.4 Tumors 
that have abnormal vessels, such as in Lhermitte-­Duclos, or 
those with evidence of prior hemorrhage, will benefit from 
susceptibility-­weighted imaging sequences, which are sensi­
tive to blood.5 Cystic tumors are generally hypointense on T1 
and hyperintense on T2 due to the liquid component; fluid-­
attenuation inversion recovery sequences can be helpful in 
tumors such as hemangioblastomas where the cystic compo­
nent is different from CSF.4 Tumors with a large percentage 
of fat-­containing substance, such as in cerebellar liponeurocy­
tomas, can be identified by hyperintense streaks on T1, and fat 
suppression sequences can aid in their diagnosis.6 The pattern 
of contrast enhancement af

ubstance, such as in cerebellar liponeurocy­

suppression sequences can aid in their diagnosis.6 The pattern

Systemic imaging should be considered for adults with an 
enhancing cerebellar mass, when clinically appropriate, to

HEMANGIOBLASTOMAS
Clinical Features
Hemangioblastomas are the most common primary tumors 
of the cerebellum in adults (76%), accounting for 1.5% to 
2.5% of intracranial tumors and 7% to 8% of posterior 
fossa tumors in adults. They can be divided into sporadic 
tumors, which accounts for approximately 75% of heman­
gioblastomas, or those associated with von Hippel-­Lindau 
(VHL) disease (10% to 40%).2 Hemangioblastomas have a 
slight male predominance in sporadic patients, and female 
predominance in VHL patients. In sporadic cases, they are 
more common in the fifth and sixth decades of life, whereas 
in VHL, patients are usually diagnosed in the second and 
third decade of life. The most common locations include 
cerebellum (>70%), brainstem (>20%), fourth ventricle 
(2%), cerebellopontine angle (2%), and

third decade of life. The most common locations include 
cerebellum (>70%), brainstem (>20%), fourth ventricle 
(2%), cerebellopontine angle (2%), and craniocervical junc­
tion (2%). Furthermore, 5% of all spinal cord primary neo­
plasms are hemangioblastomas.2–9
Hemangioblastomas are benign, well-­circumscribed, and 
highly vascular lesions. MRI features of an enhancing nodule 
associated with a peritumoral cyst in the cerebellum, with 
low T1-­weighted signal and high-­contrast enhancement, 
with flow voids on T2-­weighted imaging, raise suspicion for 
the diagnosis. Morphologically, tumors can be divided into 
solid (48%), cystic (26%), cystic with mural nodule (21%), 
and both solid and cystic (5%), with the solid type domi­
nating across both sporadic and VHL subtypes. Multiple 
lesions are almost exclusively associated with VHL.2–12

Biology
Histologic examination of hemangioblastomas shows an 
extensive vascular network with neoplastic stromal cells with 
abundant cytoplasm and lipid vacuoles with a typical clear 
cell morphology. Markers for vimentin (100%), vascular 
endothelial growth factor (VEGF; 100%), CD34 (82%), 
neuron-­specific enolase (93%), S-­100 (81%), and glial fibril­
lary acidic protein (50%) are frequently immunopositive.7
VHL disease is transmitted in an autosomal dominant man­
ner with an incidence of 1/36,000. It is caused by a mutation 
in the VHL gene on chromosome 3p25-­26, resulting in loss 
of function for the VHL tumor suppressor, which serves as a 
negative regulator of VEGF. Criteria for diagnosis of VHL 
include positive germline mutation on peripheral blood, fam­
ily history of VHL disease and VHL-­associated tumor, nega­
tive family history with two or more central nervous system

VHL-­associated tumor. Additional tumors observed in VHL 
include retinal angiomas, renal cell carcinomas pheochromo­

endolymphatic sac tumors. Neurosurgeons should be aware

newly suspected hemangioblastomas are to perform imaging

testing for metanephrines, vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), and

On histology, pilocytic astrocytomas have alternating

fusion in 70% of cases and lack the IDH1/2 mutation.23,24

Clinical Features
Ependymomas are neuroepithelial tumors that may arise 
throughout the neuraxis, with the most common site being 
the posterior fossa (60% of all tumors).64 Classically, epen­
dymomas originate in the fourth ventricle, with involve­
ment of the floor, lateral recesses, or roof, in descending 
order. The highest incidence is observed in young children, 
whereas in adults, they are a relatively infrequent diagno­
sis and manifest in the spine more commonly. Presentation 
reflects the anatomic regions of involvement or signs of 
hydrocephalus. Imaging reveals a well-­circumscribed mass 
with variable enhancement. Extension out of the foramen 
of Luschka from a fourth ventricular mass is suggestive of 
ependymoma. Upon clinical suspicion of an ependymoma, 
imaging of the entire neuraxis should

able enhancement. Extension out of the foramen 
of Luschka from a fourth ventricular mass is suggestive of 
ependymoma. Upon clinical suspicion of an ependymoma, 
imaging of the entire neuraxis should be performed, as well 
as CSF sampling. 
Biology
Classic ependymomas are considered WHO grade II, 
whereas anaplastic ependymomas are classified as WHO 
grade III, although grade does not consistently reflect 
survival in ependymoma.64 Three histologic variants are 
observed in both grades: papillary, clear cell, and tanycytic. 
Posterior fossa ependymomas demonstrate two molecu­
larly distinct subgroups: group A and group B.65 Group A 
ependymomas tend to manifest in young patients, are more 
laterally located, and have higher recurrence, metastases, 
and mortality. Interestingly, group B ependymomas tend to 
have a disrupted genome, with frequent chromosomal gains 
and losses, whereas group A ependymomas harbor a bal­
anced genome, which is contrary to the frequent association 
of genom

have a disrupted genome, with frequent chromosomal gains 
and losses, whereas group A ependymomas harbor a bal­
anced genome, which is contrary to the frequent association 
of genome disruption with more aggressive disease across 
other cancers. 
Treatment
Surgery is the first line treatment strategy for ependymo­
mas, with the extent of resection associated with patient 
outcome. Gross total resection offers the greatest survival 
advantage and may also help reestablish CSF flow in cases 
of obstructive hydrocephalus. Tissue for molecular profil­
ing may also abet subsequent prognostication. Adjuvant 
radiation, even in the setting of gross total resection, offers 
a survival advantage and improved local control at 10 years 
for posterior fossa ependymomas.66 This is distinct from 
supratentorial ependymomas, where the role of adjuvant 
radiation, especially in the setting of gross total resection, 
remains controversial.

METASTASES
Clinical Features
The cerebellum is a site of metastasis in approximately 9% 
of patients with metastatic brain tumors, with the most 
common sites of primary cancer being lung (39.4%), breast 
(22%), and gastrointestinal (17.4%).67 As the survival of 
cancer patients increases with more effective targeted and 
immunotherapies, the incidence and pattern of distribution 
of CNS metastases is likely to change as well. The cerebel­
lum is also a common site for detection of leptomeningeal 
seeding, which frequently manifests with cranial nerve palsy 
or hydrocephalus.
Cerebellar metastases are associated with worse survival 
and increased spinal recurrence after surgery, compared 
with other intracranial metastases.68 They are additionally 
associated with increased need for CSF diversion proce­
dures, either temporary or p

d increased spinal recurrence after surgery, compared 
with other intracranial metastases.68 They are additionally 
associated with increased need for CSF diversion proce­
dures, either temporary or permanent. In contrast to supra­
tentorial metastases, where surgery is frequently considered 
for solitary or oligometastases or large symptomatic tumors, 
a 3-­cm cerebellar metastasis in the setting of multiple other 
metastasis might be candidate for surgical resection if pro­
ducing significant edema or mass effect.

Cerebellar metastases require aggressive treatment. Mul­
tiple studies support surgical resection along with adju­
vant radiation therapy for prolonged survival. In a 15-­year 
analysis of 109 patients with cerebellar metastases, there 
was an increased median survival time in patients who had

Positioning for posterior fossa surgical approaches depends 
on patient habitus, patient comorbidities, and surgeon pref­

supine with a shoulder roll.
The prone position is commonly selected for both mid­

Posterior Fossa
Lesions located anteriorly on the tentorial surface of the 
cerebellum are often difficult to reach by the standard 
suboccipital approach. In addition to the supracerebel­
lar infratentorial approach, the occipital transtentorial 
approach is another alternative when resecting antero­
superior cerebellar lesions. The incision, either lin­
ear, curvilinear, or otherwise, is at the discretion of the 
surgeon. The craniotomy should allow exposure of the 
venous sinuses, taking care to avoid venous bleeding or 
injury early in the case with placement of the bur holes 
and turning of the cranial flap. The occipital pole is gently 
retracted with caution to preserve any bridging veins. A

Complications
Surgery for posterior fossa lesions is associated with risk 
related to the cerebellum, brainstem, and cranial nerves, 
as well as with perturbations in CSF flow (e.g., hydro­
cephalus or CSF leak) and venous structures. CSF leaks 
are the most common surgical complication in the poste­
rior fossa. They can be minimized with a watertight dural 
cl

in CSF flow (e.g., hydro­
cephalus or CSF leak) and venous structures. CSF leaks 
are the most common surgical complication in the poste­
rior fossa. They can be minimized with a watertight dural 
closure. Both immediately and delayed hydrocephalus can 
be observed following resection of cerebellar tumors and 
should be monitored in the postoperative setting, even after 
initial discharge from the hospital. Craniotomies for poste­
rior fossa tumors are associated with a higher incidence of 
temporary and permanent CSF diversion compared with 
those at other intracranial locations. Even in the absence 
of overt hydrocephalus, patients may also manifest with 
pseudomeningoceles under the incision. Depending on the 
size and symptoms associated with the pseudomeningocele, 
it may be monitored, drained with a compression wrap, or 
sometimes prompt a revision of the underlying closure.
Cerebellar mutism is a rare postoperative complication

Cerebellar mutism is a rare postoperative complication 
seen with resection of cerebellar tumors. This complication 
occurs in approximately 1% of cases and is observed more 
commonly in children, although cases have been reported 
in adults. Cerebellar mutism is considered a severe form of 
dysarthria; it manifests as hesitant slow speech or frank mut­
ism. In all documented cases, it is transient and associated 
with vermal tumors. Cerebellar mutism is believed to be 
related to postsurgical edema or ischemia involving the den­
tate nucleus or pathways of the dentatorubrothalamic tract.

DEFINITION 
 
Neurosurgery is the specialty of surgery dedicated to the diagnosis, surgical and non-
surgical management of congenital abnormalities, trauma and diseases affecting the 
nervous system, its blood supply, and supporting structures. 
 
 
GOALS 
 
Upon completion of training, a resident is expected to be a competent specialist in 
Neurosurgery capable of assuming a consultant’s role. The resident must acquire a thorough 
working knowledge of the theoretical basis of Neurosurgery, including its foundations in 
basic medical sciences and research. 
 
Residents must demonstrate the requisite knowledge, skills, and attitudes for effective 
patient-centred care and service to a diverse population. In all aspects of specialist practice, 
the graduate must be able to address ethical issues and issues of gender, sexual 
orientation, age, cul

atient-centred care and service to a diverse population. In all aspects of specialist practice, 
the graduate must be able to address ethical issues and issues of gender, sexual 
orientation, age, culture, and ethnicity in a professional manner. 
 
The resident must be well-grounded in the general principles of both Neurosurgery and 
surgery in general. The fully-trained resident must demonstrate proficiency and expertise in 
the care of neurosurgical conditions as well as pre- and post- surgical care. 
 
In addition to knowledge, clinical ability, and surgical skill as these apply to surgical 
diseases of the nervous system, the resident will be expected to have a working knowledge 
of the related disciplines of basic and clinical neuroscience. 
 
Residents must demonstrate a detailed knowledge of the normal structure and function of 
the nervous system and its supporting structures, and the pathological processes affecting 
them. They must demonstrate the diagnostic skills to identif

Over the past 25 years, intraoperative neurophysiology 
(ION) has established itself as a clinical discipline that uses 
neurophysiologic methods—especially developed or modi­
fied from existing methods of clinical neurophysiology—to 
detect and prevent intraoperatively induced neurologic inju­
ries. Recent developments have solidified its role in neuro­
surgery and other surgical disciplines. Ideally, ION not only 
predicts but also serves to prevent intraoperatively induced 
injury to the nervous system. Furthermore, ION can be used 
to document the exact moment when the injury occurred. As 
a result, it can be used for both educational and medicolegal 
purposes.
Generally, ION techniques can be divided in two groups: 
mapping and monitoring. Neurophysiologic mapping is a 
technique that, when applied intraoperatively, enables us 
to identify anatomically indistinct neural structures by their 
neurophysiologic function. This allows the surgeon to avoid 
lesioning critical structur

text:
hat, when applied intraoperatively, enables us 
to identify anatomically indistinct neural structures by their 
neurophysiologic function. This allows the surgeon to avoid 
lesioning critical structures in the course of the surgical pro­
cedure. In essence, the information gained from neurophysi­
ologic mapping allows the surgeon to operate more safely.
The following procedures use a neurophysiologic map­
ping technique: identification of the primary motor cortex 
with direct cortical stimulation, identification of the cranial 
nerve motor nuclei on the surgically exposed floor of the 
fourth ventricle, mapping of the corticospinal tract (CT) 
subcortically (i.e., at the level of the cerebral peduncle or at 
the spinal cord), mapping of the pudendal afferents in the 
sacral roots, before selective dorsal rhizotomy, and so on.
Neurophysiologic monitoring is a technique that con­
tinuously evaluates the functional integrity of nervous tis­
sue and gives feedback to the (neuro)surgeon. Th

Neurophysiologic monitoring is a technique that con­
tinuously evaluates the functional integrity of nervous tis­
sue and gives feedback to the (neuro)surgeon. This feedback 
can be instantaneous, as in a recently developed technique of 
monitoring motor-­evoked potentials (MEPs) from the epi­
dural space of the spinal cord or limb muscles. If the surgical 
procedure allows us to combine monitoring with mapping 
techniques, then optimal protection of nervous tissue can be 
achieved during neurosurgery.
Furthermore, ION uses provocative tests to examine 
their influence on neurophysiologic signals before the surgi­
cal procedure. A temporary clamping of the carotid artery 
during endarterectomy with monitoring of somatosensory-­
evoked potentials (SEPs) or electroencephalography is a 
typical example of a provocative test that measures the ability 
of the collateral cerebral circulation to supply a potentially 
ischemic hemisphere. Endovascular inje

typical example of a provocative test that measures the ability 
of the collateral cerebral circulation to supply a potentially 
ischemic hemisphere. Endovascular injection of a short-­
acting barbiturate or lidocaine into a vascular malformation 
of the spinal cord, before embolization, and observation 
of its influence on the neurophysiologic signals is another 
example of a provocative test.
Supratentorial Surgery
Surgery for brain gliomas has become more and more 
aggressive. This is based on clinical data that support better 
patient survival and quality of life after gross total removal of 
both low-­ and high-­grade lesions;1,2 however, the resection 
of tumors located in eloquent brain areas, such as the rolan­
dic region and frontotemporal speech areas, requires the 
identification of functional cortical and subcortical areas that 
must be respected during surgery. Moreover, the dogmatic 
assumption that tumoral tissue could not retain function

metadata.source: Intraoperative Neurophysiology- A Tool to Prevent and:or Document Intraoperative Injury to the Nervous System.pdf

reas, requires the 
identification of functional cortical and subcortical areas that 
must be respected during surgery. Moreover, the dogmatic 
assumption that tumoral tissue could not retain function has 
been repeatedly questioned by neurophysiologic and func­
tional magnetic resonance imaging studies.3–5 In response to 
the need for a safe surgery in eloquent brain areas, the past 
decade has seen the development of a number of techniques 
to map brain functions, including, but not limited to, func­
tional magnetic resonance imaging, magnetoencephalogra­
phy, and positron emission tomography.6–11
The neurophysiologic contribution to brain mapping has 
been evident since the late 19th century with the pioneering 
work of Fritsch and Hitzig12 and Bartholow.13 In the 20th 
century, Penfield and colleagues14,15 made invaluable contri­
butions through intraoperative mapping of the sensorimotor 
cortex, whose findings have been substantiated by a number 
of recent studies.16–18

DIRECT CORTICAL STIMULATION (60-­HZ PENFIELD 
TECHNIQUE)
Once the motor strip has indirectly been identified by 
the phase reversal technique, direct cortical stimulation is 
required to confirm the localization of the motor cortex. 
Most current methods are based on the original Penfield 
technique. This calls for continuous direct cortical stimu­
lation over a period of a few seconds with a frequency of 
stimulation of 50 to 60 Hz and observation of muscle move­
ments.14,16,27 An initial current intensity of 4 mA is used 
and, if no movements are elicited in contralateral muscles 
of the limbs and face, stimulation is increased in steps of 2 
mA to the point at which movements are elicited.16 Muscle 
responses can either be observed visually or documented by 
multichannel electromyography, which appears to be more 
sensitive.28 If no response is elicited with an intensity as high

The short train of stimuli technique delivers five to seven 
stimuli in a period of approximately 30 ms with a long pause

WARNING CRITERIA AND CORRELATION WITH 
POSTOPERATIVE OUTCOME
Still debated are the warning criteria for changes in muscle 
MEPs that are used to inform the surgeon about an impend­
ing injury to the motor system. It should be stressed that 
although for spinal cord surgery, a “presence/absence” of 
muscle MEPs criterion has proved to be reliable and strictly 
correlates with postoperative results,44,45 there are not defi­
nite MEP parameters indicative of significant impairment 
during supratentorial surgery.46 We believe that the pre­
dictive value of muscle MEPs is different for supratentorial 
and spinal cord surgeries. As such, different warning criteria 
must be employed. This judgment is based on the differ­
ence in types of CT fibers in supratentorial portion of the 
CT as compared with the spinal cord. Different groups with 
established experience in this field have proposed similar cri­
teria,40,46 suggesting that a shift in latency between 10% and 
15% and a decrea

established experience in this field have proposed similar cri­
teria,40,46 suggesting that a shift in latency between 10% and 
15% and a decrease in amplitude of more than 50% to 80% 
correlate with some degree of postoperative motor deficit. 
However, a permanent new motor deficit has consistently
